speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This interview with Frank Herzog was recorded at his home in Harvard on July 18, 1975. The interviewer was Sam Schrager. The poor sound quality on side A of this tape was corrected for the remainder of the interview. Well, where did you trap mostly?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Right around here, in Harvard. We trapped muskrat, deer, coyotes… i wanted to last, but that's my father trapped there all the time we was here in the spring. The last year my brother and I was going to school up here while we took over and trapped in the… that year they paid $10 bounty on the bear. We had four traps. We went over to the woods and here over to the head of the bear. We caught 10 at the spring. We figured that's going to keep the bounty on them. Then we took our traps up and trapped them in the spring when the fur was good. But next year it took the bounty off.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: A hundred bucks sounds like a lot of money to get.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: We didn't want to trap them on the fur. The bear was a killing stock, I guess, in places that were eating the put the bounty on. I don't know. Something probably wouldn't want to pay in there. It's silly the way the game information is protecting the coyotes and the bears. They're killing all the deer and elk. They haven't got brains enough to know it. Just lately they are investigating it. I think this year they found 14 elk calves had been killed and the bear had killed for 12. They found the same thing last year. Why and what really is a bear? They found out one of them was going to fit in each. Oh, at that time, you know, there was lots of horses. There was no one. There were tracks or anything like that. Everything was fine. Everything was old and was good. Everything was horse. That would be a lot of old horses that were too old to work. I wanted to get rid of them and we'd get them and take them out in the woods and kill them using for coyote bait.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I'm ready to wait for the coyotes to work in them. Oh, and lots of magpies and buzzards. I used to call them turkey buzzards. You couldn't set your tracks close to the horse because you did get magpies. They had the same materials coming in to it. You could nail them when they were coming in. We caught the highest four or five in the night. The other stuff was in the wintertime. Why wait until they got to work and the horse grew. You could get rid of them. When it started snowing real hard, go out and set your tracks in the trails and brush them over. You got to back up and brush out your tracks with a pusher or a lean tree. When it's low, cover everything up later in the morning and you'd have a lot of trouble.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you say the trail, do you mean a walking trail or an animal trail?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Not to me. You take your horse out and kill it. You put it for a lot of trails leading into a certain point. I always had the idea that coyotes are pretty wily, pretty smart animals.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is that the truth, do you think?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: It really is after you've trapped them a while. Right now, I could go out and trap coyotes that haven't been trapped. You see around here for years, I could go out and catch them right and left. But after a bit, when they seen those other coyotes and those traps, then they get wise and pretty foxy. I had a trap set in the snow in the trail. I had the coyote walk up to the trap and he smelled it right through that snow and he walked out of the runs. When you set a trap, you have to be set natural. You dig a hole in the ground and set your trap down so it's level with the trail and cover it with whatever is around there so it looks natural. It's got to look natural if it doesn't, you're not going to get no coyote. And another stunt, they take setting in a trail where they go down in the draw or not. You set the trap on each side and catch them when they're coming in. If they're going up that hill on the trail, they'll smell your trap and go around.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: They'll normally go to the ground, see?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would you bait them with? What? Would you bait the traps?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No, a trail set you need to... Of course, you can use sand and draw to your trap too. What you can do is take some of this practitioners and put them in a bottle and hang it up in the sun so it gets brighten. And then use that and I'd probably knock you down when you open the bottle. The coyote smells like sleep, that's probably bad for a second. On an old bear, he will eat anything. He'll take an old horse or something that's just rolling with maggots and stuff and he'll come and eat the whole thing. When they trap and bear two good stumps, they'll go and have some old apples in the spring beak. They can put a few in the sack and where we set our trap, we mash them, chop them, hang them up in the tree. And if they'll actually, a mile or more, come right to it. I've had a trap set where it was grassy and then we, where we set our trap, we use a piece of old horse meat or a little honey and oil to ban us. But it's not made of camp.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Then we find a brush pile or something and spread it apart in a V shape, you know, and thick wool or service or something up on the edges. And then set your trap in there and put your bait back in there. I never heard of but one that was hard to trap. He'd come up and work his paw under that trap and set it out to one size when you have to bait. Don't let it dry. The second time he did it, I took one trap up. The next trap I had set, I took it up and brought it back. And I set one trap real good so we couldn't see it. It was just nice. And the other one I set it right in front of it and set it so we could see it. You could see it through his attacks. Now he comes up and he lifts this one up and sets the little one side and finds it and put it right in the next one. He didn't know it was too loud. And he had two toes off. He'd been trapped before.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Somebody had caught him and probably set the trap wrong. We used to stick sharp sticks up around the trap. They put the foot and wouldn't step on them sharp sticks. They'd step right in there. Nice, smooth place. You see the trap has got a big trigger where it goes over the jaw and hooks underneath the pan. And you both turn that around in the opposite direction. So if he comes in here and he steps on that trigger, it throws his foot up in the air. Never then, that's what somebody set the trap that way. It threw his foot up and just got two toes. The other way always is to jaw in the pan and he's bound to get it. Well, we had to... Just like they say, as clumsy as a bear. People that say that, they don't know what they're talking about. Because I see we had a yellow dog, he's part hound, part air -dale. And he could... I had a good saddle horse and he doesn't have the wrong side of me. The horse going to the back, he'd go. But we had a bear in the trap and just as we got there, he was on the open hillside. He got loose, got the clogged loose. We always fastened a tree that big around and it was probably 10, 12 feet long. We cut the limbs off that long, you see. So he could follow it. That way, they took someplace and get hung up.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: There he got that clogged loose and just took down that open hillside. Now, you can see where the black and yellow streets at go right at me… where's that trap… i'm on front foot. You're going like that. Then we got him. Climb a tree. Climb a tree and be up there on the wind with that big trap. I'm on front foot and that's all.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How can they..… you got the trap chained down though, don't you? How do they get the trap out to move away?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I don't know. I didn't see him climbing, but I don't know if he's counting down. And there. Oh, there it is. It's pretty much hard because it's going to go in one direction and that's it. I've had him run that clog around the tree like that. They could have come around this way, come back around this way if he got loose. No, they stay right there. They want to go that way. I'm focusing on the whole thing.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you chain the trap around the tree? Was there a chain on the trap to hold it there so he couldn't move?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Well, if you... As a rule, your set probably isn't focused enough to a tree. And if you didn't set it there, why then... Before you had your trap set, you just ruined everything, tear it all down. Or if you put a clog on and get in, he'll take off. And you can kill him and bring your trap back inside. You can't get away with that big clog. No, you're talking about a chain out of the tree -ache chain on a bear trap. Three -eight -sixth chain with a swivel in it and a ring that big around it. You put it on the tree, you take and flip that ring over it and flip the tree and drive in the big wedge. We can't get the ring back off of it. And drive it in that way so it won't come out.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How often would you check the traps, those bear traps, every day?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I suppose it should have been checked every day, but we were doing the school we went once a week. Maybe some of them have been in the trap two -four -eight. But if it was somebody out that had the time to go and look at them, why... Look at them every two days anyway. We'll check out traps here close, we make mud -strap traps, we'll check those every day.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would one of those bears, if he'd been in the trap for a few days when you got out there, too, and would he still be alive and mad? Mad? Would they be furious? Would they be mad?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Some of them. But the most of them, all they think about is the gateway. We caught one that had just hung up, beside him, a big yellow, never -fine windfall. It had big, big schnapps on it like that, you know. They just had started to rock. He was mad. He grabbed them big knots and ring them off. He done that until he had all his teeth pulled out. But he didn't pour enough of his snow. Well, if I had only eaten, when he tracked the bear, he'd never carry the gun. He said that we'd get too much for a way to pack. He'd cut him a club about ten, twelve feet long and kill him all that. And I'm over the head. There wasn't very many deer in this country at that time. I was talking on YouTube. We'd see a deer. There was a bunch of new deer up here on ... Hill that we had spotted before. Kill the night before...

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: There was no season then over the season at that time. They didn't have to buy our license for that. But there was quite a few people that trapped coyotes and bears. They kept them down, you know, when there wasn't a thing. But now the bear and coyotes are getting so thick they're following the game.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you have places that you set and reset the same bear trap? Were there special places where you picked out for them or would you move them around?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Should have backed the same place. Nothing bothered me… you see it… bears travel throughout the country. Every so often they've got a tree that they mark. There's a scratch it, bite it, a rub on it. Every bear that comes along with that tree. And if you're wise to that, you can follow it. But to the coach, you can set your trap so I'm not riled for a bit more. I saw up here on that sand creek divide where there was a bear. The tree was all marked up where there had been marks in it. But there was one that had reached up, you know, I'm six feet tall and I had to reach up like that to touch it before he bit the chunk out. And it was a small tree. I know he didn't climb it to bite it. I'd like to get a hold of that. Did you see how big it really was? Well, that was another thing they do here every once in a while. Somebody around the country is seeing a wolf. There is no wolves in this country. It's just that they were overgrown coyotes. We caught one that measured over five feet. You know these fur houses, they used to have grades extra large, large, medium, and small on their list. There used to be lots of them. And that's the only hide we ever got that we got extra large for.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: And they just overgrown coyotes just like anything else. I saw a mule deer once that was killed. And they said that it was hanging up in the meat market in the wind. They said it dressed 498 pounds. And it looked like it too. It looked like an elf. Big mule butt. And it's all full dark brown. And everything is something like that on ..., extra large.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How much trapping did you do when you were a kid?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I got a week right every winter when the fur was good.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did your father teach you? Is that how you learned from your father? Did he teach you boys how to do it? Did your father teach you boys how to do it?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: The deer..… it's a trap on the case experience. The more you're trapped, the more you learn, just like anything else. I still got 3 bear traps. I was offered $35 a piece for them. I don't think you can buy one now. I sold a whole bunch. About a year ago. In fact, what good of it was the trap bear. All we are is an ornament to hang up on the fence or something like that. I showed my shoulder and something.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember how old you were when you started going out with your father and looking at the trap?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: My father… i was probably 12, 14 years old.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you think the blood bothered you at first? Did the animals get trapped? Did they get used to it?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No… you said blood?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you were a kid, I was thinking of just a little kid going out.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No, I was not a brother. I've seen guys that have done it. I saw one of the big fellas. He couldn't be around when he was butchering a hog or a beef. See that blood, he just hit the ground.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you just leave the meat most of the time? Did people eat the meat? Did you just leave it?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I just try to chomp on quarters sometimes. Take the throw and snort it. You used to hunt the hogs and bees, eat yours.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you think there was much luck involved in trapping or was it just a skill of knowing where to put them?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No luck, whatever. It's all skill and know -how experience. No such a thing as being lucky. Just by trapping me. The less scent you leave around that trap, the more you know how to set that trap, the more meat you're going to catch. A lot of them will pass it up if it isn't set right. And if it can, set in the water that isn't freezing. And then cover your trap up with water so clean that it will go over your trap. And also get in the water and splash your whole set with water. It has a tendency to kill the sandals. And you used to cut a well with a hook on it like that. Otherwise ... could chew their foot right off. They're in the trap and they want to time it. Chew the seagull.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you do good trapping minks here? Was there a lot of minks?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Oh, I wouldn't say a lot, but it was quite a few. There was a more of a trap to either guess what they got. When they first started eating water, it was quite a lot. And there was no beaver.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Really?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Not a beaver. In all the trap, we even got here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, they say there was guys in here trapping before the gold miners even came. I suppose beaver was what they were looking for more than anything else.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Oh, they trapped everything as far as that goes, but they cleaned out the beaver. That's another thing the game commissioned, that rotten in there. They let these trappers go way back up on these creeks and trap those beaver out. They should be left alone. One that's down here is doing damage. That's all right, the trap's in. Way back in the hills, there used to be quite a lot of beaver back up in the hills, but they're getting them old trap tabs.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What good do the beavers do back there?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Well, they pull the water back from the summertime. It gives you more water, you know. Then the ponds are all full of fish. Good for the fish. There's an animal, I tell you. One year I worked on a forest in this, that was up on the east forest of the potlatch. The beaver didn't put in the dam and flooded the trail. We was cutting out trails.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: We thought it was pretty hard to move the trail because the hill was steep and rocky, see?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: We thought we'd tear the beaver dam out. They had that dam right in the swift ripples too. We got in there and tore it all out.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The next morning it was for their build -up again, right?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: That swift ripples. I couldn't get out there and fast mistake in that ripples, but they did.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you do?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: You'd last the same. Nobody said tearing it out again and just build it up again.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about cougar, Frank? You run into them at all?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No. I've been around where they were at quite a lot. I was working in the woods then. But in the early days there was very few cougars around there. This is getting to be quite a lot now. Do they protect them? There was quite a few people around that had hounds. They would run there and cougar. Oh, we used to trap the link. There was quite a lot of link and they cut you. Then, and now I don't think there's one. Every once in a while we'd get one of those big links and they're a bear trap. We didn't want to kill them because their fur was worth a lot of money if they lived. So, the leg would be broke. We'd try to fork its stick and stand by their neck and pin them down and finish stopping their leg off and letting them go. They'd hatch it and just be tenets and hide and stuff for holding them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever catch any of those ones again? The ones you'd cut one leg off later?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No. I don't know what they lived now. Maybe they did hold one. Well, I had, I had caught several coyotes and one leg off her foot. So, I don't see why the link couldn't fit too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think there's more game now than there was in or less?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Well, there's lots more elk and deer. In fact, then there wasn't any elk. There was a few deer scattered around, but now there's. A few years ago, there was lots of deer around here. A hard winter and coyotes. Here is the idea. A coyote had a thing to live on in the wintertime, except in this country, except in game.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Now, what game is this?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Birds, pheasants, and droughts, and deer. No rabbit. There isn't any rabbit. There was lots of rabbits. They would live on rabbits. But they're killing deer in the winter. That's what they're living on. You're taking that deep snow, especially if there's a little crust on it. Then they got the deer and he... He would go to the crust and they would run on top of it. And then finally run him until he's down, then chew his hands out while he's still alive. And then go and do the same thing to another one. I'll kill several deer and drug yourselves down into the road with their hands he'd have. They look that poisonous. Or put a bounty on them. If they go and put a bounty on them, why is it I grew up trapping myself? Especially in the summertime, you know. This winter trapping without a bait was kind of tough. The trap deep snowed in and froze in and everything. In the summertime, I would just be picking for a while. And they would say, you could just thought around.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: These guys that use hounds, honey, was that just mostly for sport? They didn't get the quantity that you could get trapping, could they? With hounds?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Nah, they don't seem to be so successful. They're going to try and work like this to get more foxy in the hounds. Unless they can get where these hounds were to run and one of them and they can chew it. There's a little tick off from Google that I was getting country. Because nearly a year or so ago there were several outfits that had hounds down there around Princeton. With the chasing coyotes, but I know that they didn't have much success. Once in a while they'd get more.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you do that when you were trapping? Did you use hounds too?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No, we never had them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where did your father pick it up, the trapping? You know how he learned it?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: He started out in Pennsylvania. He had a lot of trapping in Pennsylvania. He came out here and had his tick on. There's getting to be quite a few wildcats around here now. I don't know for sure, but I believe that the lake killed the wildcat. Because it wasn't. He never got a wildcat. He was a tracking lake. And there was no sign of a coon in this country and now it's getting a big wild deer. Well, I guess so. But he didn't just make a business of trapping. He worked in the woods sometimes in the farm. Of course in the wintertime there wasn't much to do on the farm, so he trapped. I really don't know of anybody that was in this country that just made a business of trapping.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you quit it when spring come along?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Boy… after the fur got no good. I'm missing you, chat. That spring was just there when they come out.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've heard that your father was a pretty tough guy. He was a strong guy.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: He was a big man. Hard worker. He didn't take anything off from anybody. We're all looking for trouble.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Somebody mentioned to me that, I think maybe it was Glenn, he cut his toe off.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Kind of what?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He cut his toe off.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: That was up here on the farm. He was a slash and a tree. He's brushing stuff to clear up land, you know, before we burned it. Then I asked Glenn to try to tow him too. He took his shoe off and looked at it. So he put it back on and went to work. That's a bone sticking up there. He brought it back and he took that and cut that bone off so it wouldn't stick up on his shoe. That's what I remember that day. Later on, I suppose there was a chip of that bone in there that kept bothering him. So he took a piece of pliers and yanked it out. And it healed up all right. All those days when something like that happened, he didn't run to the doc.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where was your place where you lived, Dan? Have you been up the road here?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: You know, there's a barn set right on the lower side of the road. Yeah. And I go over the hill and we built that barn in 1916. And I put those shakes on this side of it. Just a kid. I'll bet it still doesn't leak. My brother and I hauled those shakes from way up ... Creek. What is it called? Cedar Grove. This is no cedar there now. It was a whole lot of great big cedar things. And the house stood on the upper side of the road. The long house he built when he comes there. He built a house. But the place was sold in a toilet house, Dan.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When did he come out here?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Moved to the Palouse in 1900. About 75 years ago.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he know?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I think I was, I was even. A year and a half or two years old somewhere around there. I was born in Pennsylvania.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he know about this place from back there? Or did he just find it when he came out here?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Well, he came out here the year before we moved out. He came out here and he worked in the hay fields up here. He was having rheumatoid real bad. And I guess the doctor stoned me to change climate. So he came out here to look around the year before and look in the hay fields up here. He got the feeling real good. So he decided he went back and then next year removed that. So he came out here and he was in the hay fields up here. You know, when we came here, there was no car. No pot lags. No railroad. Just an old Caledary road. Dirt. Make a trip. No, no, I had a truffle tendency to get rid of poos and the team wagons. There was a fire mill in Palouse and it run on water. Get this engine out. Get a couple barrels of flour… make a fit… these are two dollars or two dollars and a half for a hundred pounds of flour.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Flour used to be putting cotton sacks, you know, in the 250 pound bags in a gun set.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you growing wheat at the time and on your place? Did you have any wheat to take down there?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No, not then… he's mostly hay and cattle. At that time there was very little grain. Greatness country. We run heavy to Timothy and Clover hay because there were so many horses in the country and horses in all the logging camps. They'd sell their hay. Grain with sheep. Wheat. At that time, if the farmers got 50 cents a bushel for their wheat, they thought they'd get a big price.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You grew up right by Glen Gilder then, right? That's where Glen Gilder grew up too, right? Right neighbor to you.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: We've gone over on the hill there a ways.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think your father had to work real hard to get by here in them early days?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Everybody did. Not only him, but all the rest of them. He worked up in the logging camps around here. Ten hours a day. I'm not sure now what the wages were, but I know there wasn't a dollar and a half for two dollars a day. He was really good with an axe, broad axe. He'd get a shoot. I do something that's a lot of good now. A long shoot. He'd do that timber for barns. He'd do the tights. Well, I'm only got, there was only a ten, two and a half a day then. But that is starting in with the eight hours and bunk houses around here in these old, oh, I told you about them, old logging camps before.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: A little bit about them. You told me a little bit about them. You said they were pretty lousy.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Just a big log shack. A great big stove right in the middle of the shack. No floor in them. Pilots draw the sleep on them. Before it was my dad, he didn't stay in any of them. He walked back and forth home and go to work.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've heard about those camps in the Midwest, Minnesota, Wisconsin being really tough places where guys get drinking and they fight and the guy get knocked down and get it with the other guy and give it to him with his corp boots. Was there much of that around here?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Not too much. The most of that was done in town at the saloons. The camps, they didn't have the most trouble that way. Too much work and too tired to do that kind of stuff. Well, getting town to go in was a lot of it going on. I've even seen that… all around 1923,… 1924. That and Clarkia up here used to be a wild place. I've heard they didn't have prohibition there just about in Clarkia. That's right. It was wide open. There was a saloon. Moonshine right over the counter. Didn't seem to bother them any. Every weekend I come in from those camps and be able to get drunk and fight.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would the fights be over anything or just over being drunk?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Well, they'd get in arguments and then it'd wind up in a fight. Then some of them I'd just go around looking for it. See which is the best man. It was a big bridesmaids, I think, was the best man around the country. The name was Wes Allen. He went and spoke in and cleaned up all the pubs and spoke in too in the back alley.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you think he fought much around here? Did he have to fight much to prove it? Did he was tough?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: There wasn't much of it around here. It was dry around here. There was nothing wide open like that. In the early days when the saloons was open, I think he had three or four saloons in Princeton. There was a lot of fighting going on down there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you know Wes Allen?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I seen him. I was never around for it. My brother knew him well. He told me a lot about him. I never appointed him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Your brother thought he was really the toughest man in the country, though, huh?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Yeah… i mean, he did. I wonder how a guy gets a reputation like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He must have cleaned up on quite a few to get it, huh?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: He was just like it was at that time in Spokane. I think here there's a guy in town that thought he was a little better than some other bird -doyer. They'd go and hook him up. They'd go and hunt on Trent in the back alley. They'd go back and have it out. It's just like I was working up there in the camp between Beaulieu and Clarkia. There were two guys coming in there to work at that and being the same bulkhouse as I was. I don't remember where they were from, but they were telling how dead the damn place was. There was no excitement or anything. I just let them talk for a little while. I said, I'll tell you guys. If you were looking for excitement, I said, trouble, you just go down to Clarkia Saturday night. I said, this isn't very far. I said, you probably find anything you want down there. By God, we didn't do that. So they did. They come out back Sunday and remember the hell of a looking mess. It's out what they're looking for.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Black eyes and face all cut up. I didn't hear any more of that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they talk to you about it? Did they talk about what happened to it?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No. I bet they didn't. Never anymore said about it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I imagine there must have been at least one good whorehouse up there at Clarkia too.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Two of them… two of them… one on each side of Main Street. One of them was burnt down. That was a pretty big hotel on the left hand side.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you cross the tracks and go?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: It is all burnt down now. What about, I've heard that there wasn't much for drinking in the camps. No. No. It wasn't. At least I never saw much of it. You can't load up on that stuff and work. You don't feel like it. You can start getting more drinking in the evening after work around these sawmills and the woods in the woods. Of course, there's a sawmill, there's a town, and all they got to do was go to the beer parlor or the wiper store.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever see that Dick Farrell? The guy they call the lumberjack preacher? Was he ever there when he was in the woods?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I remember would happen to be in the camp that he come into. That was more of the early days along the Coeur d 'Alene. In those places I think, I've heard my brother speak about him, the old C. and Eton from the end of the camp. But I never did.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever know that Pat Malone?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Old Pat Malone. Yes. Big old fat Irishman that was supposed to be a cop of Bovill. But just he was not had any. I knew a lot of those old timers up around both.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: People remember Pat about how he, people remember all the drinking he used to do and this trying to track down, finding clues to track down the cases never catching anybody. They used to say about Pat, you know, he couldn't track an elephant in four foot of snow.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Old Pat, I don't know how many people arrested him. He might have cooked in the summer. I think his drink gets as much moonshine as the rest of them could. I worked in one camp in 1919. It's down from Helmer towards the Potlatch River there. One day the cook and the flunky said, all got drunk and quit. I don't know, we, suspicion something that they must have made it themselves. And finally found out all right, they had two or four barrels of wine in the cook house. Oh, Gil Pippen was running the camp and he went and locked it up so he couldn't get in there. So we went to the blacksmith shop and got his camp was real cars, you know, they'd just make a siding and run the cars in there, a whole bunch of bunk houses and cook houses. So we went to the blacksmith shop and got an auger and a bracing bed. And went down underneath that cook house and started boring holes to win.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Two or four guys there with their water buckets out of the bunk houses. We got quite a lot of wine, we got one barrel when we drank it. They made out of raisins. Some of them drank so much that it made them sick. I was a little wary of the stuff, I didn't drink much of it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you do with no cook or flunkies? What did you can't do without that to get somebody else in real fast? Was there much gambling in the camps we used there? Was there much gambling, poker?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Oh yeah, in that camp there was quite a lot of it. See there was gyppoing man in 1919. And there was several guys there, four or five teams. They're making good money. They had a pretty good poker game in the evening.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you do with that? You think gyppoing did much..… remember about... Joe!

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I don't know what he... I was never around him very much. He was... I held a nice old fella, you know. I worked in one of the camps for his son, one of them. Chuck worked there. And if one thing happened, he... was a guy in there, and I put all Chuck's wells right side of him to eat in at the table, see. And... this guy asked him to pass him something. He looked around and he says, I wouldn't pass nothing to a damn nigger. Well, old Chuck, he didn't say nothing, but some other guy sitting back there, he reached and got it and give it to him. But... One of them was over, and when they got through eating old Chuck, he left before this guy did, outside of the bunkhouse. He went out of the cookhouse and stood there and waited for him to come out. And when he came out, they sang, oh, no, Chuck, you beat hell out of him.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: And that tickled everybody in camp because they liked it. And they grew up with him. Old Joe Wells was... When he died, I think he had the biggest funeral ever had in Deary… and that's it… ha… i never... don't know too much about him because I... I never lived in Deary, but just working out of that in the camps.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's a good story about Chuck. I've never heard that before. I've heard he was a pretty tough guy, Chuck.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Well, I don't know. That's the only time I know of him getting in trouble. The only time I know of him, he might have been in a dozen times. But he was a nice guy. There's no reason for him. Well, that guy, he might have been a Southerner, you know. All the Southerners, they'd just taken nigger.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You didn't think too much of Big Gil, did you? Of what?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Big Gil, as a foreman. Oh, Gil was... All right. I don't know why. What makes you think that?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Because I thought when we talked the other time, he said something about him. He was a coward.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Yeah. That didn't hurt. He didn't be in the foreman. He was a good foreman. I'll tell you one thing about old Gil. They had a highline there. And it was... Of course, the highline has a trolley running on another line. Well, in some reason, the other... I didn't have nothing to do with it. I was just kidding with the team. I wanted to get that trolley up on the hill. I don't know why. But there was three big Swedes rattling around with it, trying to get it up there. Old Gil Pippen, he walked over there and picked it up and carried it up the hill. I know it weighed at least 350 pounds. He'd take a peavey, pick it up in one hand, and spin it around socket and a log, and break the handle right out of it with one hand.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, in what way was he a coward then?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No, he and... They claimed that he and another guy got in a little argument and a little guy chased him out of the woods. I didn't see it, that I heard it several times. He wouldn't fight.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He wouldn't fight, but he'd carry a 350 pound up the hill.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Yeah. And pull that, break a peavey handle up with one hand.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Geez, that's funny… i've heard he didn't talk hardly. He was really a quiet man.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Yeah, he never had much to say. Just walk around and look. He only had one eye. I don't know how he lost his eye. Maybe that's the reason he only fights.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did that accident happen to you in the woods? How did that accident happen to you in the woods? Me?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I was hooking on a double jammer, double drum jammer. I was skiddin', you know. They just shut it off, got a whole bunch of logs piled up, and then stopped. And they were going to change the lines. Of course the jammer was running, making a big racket. Evidently, while we'd been skiddin', we'd loosened up a tree. She'd probably hit it and loosened it up. Well, that damn thing fell, and I didn't hear it. Nobody heard it. I had my back to it, and it didn't make no noise. It hit me right in the head. It was one of those things. Of course, that old jammer was still running, idling and making a noise. But the tree didn't make no noise. There was no warning.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did it knock you unconscious?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Not quite… it almost... That blood poured out of my mouth and nose. It cracked my head, tore my back off. It hit me hard enough to bust a wall of my ankle. I had to put that in the cast. There's nothing touching my ankle.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you break your back with that?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No, I didn't. I didn't know what it broke. It just drove me together, like my neck, too, up here next to my shoulders. And then you get older then, when it shows up.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think, Frank, that that happened, too? A lot of guys in the woods, I mean, they got injuries that hurt them later?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Oh, yeah. They can't get banged up in that. It'll show up later on, I think, and they get older every time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How long did you work in the woods around Deary in that area?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Well, I started out 1917,… but part of it I put in around Caulfield. I worked in the woods and farmed up there, several years, and then I came back down here and went to work. My heart got worse then… my job, they had worked in the woods ever since that school. I was 65, but I still worked when I was 65. I signed up for Social Security,… and part of the time I didn't get any because I made too much money. Well, that's been ten years ago. I quit then. My back would start from the bottom and it'd end. Of course, part of the time I was making poles and you leaned over a hue and a bark off the poles, you know, and it got to get in my back until I quit. But another guy and I, we were working on our own and that bought a little piece of timber from the state. He had a cap. We had to make the poles and took the logs off.

speaker: Unknown Speaker
words: I don't know if I'll have to stay till five or not.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Oh, you going down to the post office? Well, we made about fifty dollars a day while we was working up there. That job. I was doing the falling out in the woods. And the chain saw. That was... Got rid of a lot of hardboard, cross -chain saw. The pruning had a little crosscut. I run out of them a whole lot. But this cat logged on it. It's ruling on the country. And the logged with horses, well, they didn't hurt any of the young stuff. Only those kidding trails. Didn't hurt a thingy, a mozal thingy. But now they log tree lengths and they just take everything. Hook that whole winch onto a tree and everything comes in front of it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever hear the story about Mr… kinman… i don't know which Kinman it was, but it was when Potlatch was first logging. And they decked their logs on his place. And he made them pay for using his place. Did you ever hear that story? Before he let them take the logs off of the place, he said, you're going to have to pay me.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Who was it?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Kinman… this is when they first started logging.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: It could have happened. I suppose it was the old man. I never heard anything about it. I did know that he made them boom riverbanks up there when they were driving, because the logs just turned the banks down.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You remember that family? When we were talking before, I mentioned that family. It was a family where the mother was sort of crazy. And so they kept it to themselves.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: And so they kept it to themselves. The whole family was a little bit off. Yeah, they let back up in the jungle, certainly. They done a lot of trapping in the wintertime, the ... boys. They're all dead now. Only other time they'd get out, there was... Oh, I don't know what you'd call it. A lot of self -consciousness or something. You couldn't even, you'd start to talk on the one you couldn't even get him to look at you. The only time that they went out and worked, that I know of, a couple of them worked for a brother -in -law in the hay fields.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you think of it? You think it was them, it was the way they felt, more than the way that the people felt about them?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: The people didn't bother them anything. They never bothered anybody, even bet on that. You'd sneak around, all of them but one, that's used out in the woods. You'd have to meet one of them, or you'd see a common, he'd run in height.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you think of it? Did that happen with crazy people very much? Like their mother, they just stayed at home and they didn't go to an asylum or something like that?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: They never bothered anybody or anything, so I guess there's nobody putting a holler or something. What would be the idea of sending them to asylum? They'd look like somebody that's crazy or violent or something like that, that wasn't that way. They would just want nothing that would come to town and get the mail and buy a few groceries if you had the money. Oh, they had two cattle and I raised a good garden up there. They had another on some track, I guess that's the way they made the river. The whole is going to be 95 years old.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I was going to ask you to explain one thing that you said when I was up here before. You said that corporations are ruining the country. I wondered how you mean that, that they're ruining it.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Well, they're ruining the country. Anything that they want to get. If big corporations are into everything. Well, for instance, take the big oil outfit today. They don't know. They're not only in the oil business, they're in everything. And if they see a little something that might harm them in a way, well, they're going to buy it. That shouldn't be allowed. Just like this shale coal in Wyoming and Montana. They afraid some other outfit might get it right in there and buy it all. Well, I thought, for another instance, look in California when they had the streetcars in Los Angeles and San Francisco in a big city. What did they do? They went in and bought the streetcars and put in buses. So they would use gas. Now look at the pollution they got. Don't you call that ruin the country? Them and the automobile outfit are in together. They're all in together. And they're just arriving things.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What do you think of an outfit like Potlatch? Do you think that Potlatch helped the country more or hurt the country more?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: I think they can make some jobs. It might be open. In the early days, they brought a lot of jobs.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Right… but they also wrecked a lot of country.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Oh, yeah. I'll tell you another thing about the Potlatch. They are more or less in a way rather than a state. They're taking as far as timber and stuff that's going because, well, I don't know whether you have been up that road up the Pooh's River to the Hoodoo. Well, that road was put in there for the state and gravel, crushed rock, just for the Potlatch. Otherwise, it had never been put in there. And then another instance of the Helmer. They put a good road in over across the Potlatch River and put in a big bridge there and put on crushed rock. And that's where the Potlatch is going to pull a lot of logging over there, got the logs out. Otherwise, it's no one or two families lived over in there. Otherwise, there wouldn't have been a road over there. That was all it was for. And you can see it around Lewis and Grangeville down in that country. They're getting all the road money.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: So the Potlatch just logs up around Pierce and headquarters, putting in good roads for them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you were in the camps, did they talk about Weyerhaeuser or at all in the early days? You know, the Weyerhaeuser or the guy that owns, or he used to own Potlatch.

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Oh, yeah, they do yet. Most of it. There might be a few other stockholders. They're only a big control of the interest in it. The Forestry. I can't understand why they're cutting all of this second growth. The ... little stuff… i think… i can't remember just what year it was, but I was working for Arch Kinman down here. He was logging. He had a job up on Big Creek. We went up there and they just marked the trees that we were to cut. It was quite a job. He couldn't go and broke on it just on that account because they left the most of it. Then a few years later on, they turned right around and cut the whole works… little and big… and if we, at that time, if we skinned up a tree someplace little, it had to fit. The Potlatch can go out and tear everything down and it's alright. Now, better not get in the big outfit. They do the same thing, too, now.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you see where last year, I think it was, that the Palouse District said that they'd have to use highly logging in some places?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: And they threw a fit, but I guess they didn't back down. Yeah, but they did the small part of it now that got it, so they'd have to do that. I read it in my paper. They did that, but that blog the whole works that way, but now they've got it down, so they just broke the log a small part of it that way.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you used to do much fishing in these creeks?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: Oh, yeah, there used to be lots of fish there. You could go out and catch them. Now, the kids, you'd go out and catch a nice fish. You'd mess a fish any time on the river down there. And in the real early days, before we come here, I first tell about it, you could go down to that river and shut down and take a watchtub with you and fit all the fish into just one hole. Now, you can hardly find the fish unless it's an old planter and they ain't fit to eat. I went and caught a bunch of them one year and tried to eat them and they always get by eating a bunch of mush. I used to go for years to go back, way back on Micah Creek, and catch those cut soaps in that cold water. In other words, you want something to go deep, but there's so much difference. But I've had it closed now for two or three years and I'm back then.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You think there's anything that we can do about the corporations?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: They let them get too big to be a stop to buy up everything. Running out of the old little dog, there should be a stop put to it. Well, I agree with you. 100%. That's what I figured was the trouble to this country, just like farming. They're getting to be all big farms and no little ones. The riches are buying these farms and then they claim to lose money on them when they don't. When they get that off in the income tax. All kinds of schemes. There's too much crooked work going on in the country. Everything, grass, and crooks.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You think it was the same way when you were young?

speaker: Frank Herzog
words: No.
